results.title: GitHub - jy-yuan/KIVI: [ICML 2024] KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache · GitHub
results.content:
KIVI is a new plug-and-play 2bit KV cache quantization algorithm without any fine-tuning. This algorithm optimizes memory usage by quantizing the key cache per-channel and the value cache per-token to 2bit. KIVI's hardware-friendly design allows LLMs like Llama-2, Falcon, and Mistral to maintain comparable quality levels while reducing peak memory usage by 2.6 times. This enables up to 4 times larger batch sizes and significantly increases throughput by 2.35 to 3.47 times in real LLM inference [...] real LLM inference workloads, effectively addressing the bottleneck issues in speed and memory usage. The KIVI paper highlights around 2.6x lower peak memory including weights, up to 4x larger batch size, and 2.35x–3.47x throughput gains on real inference workloads.

## What changes between the two methods

TurboQuant and KIVI both target KV cache memory, but they optimize for different points on the accuracy, complexity, and compression tradeoff curve. TurboQuant adds more math to reduce distortion; KIVI keeps the method simpler and more directly tied to 2-bit cache compression. [...] ## How to choose in practice

01

### Check your real bottleneck

If weights dominate memory, KV cache quantization may not move deployment economics much. If long contexts dominate, both methods become more relevant.

02

### Check implementation availability

A theoretically better paper result is not enough if your runtime stack does not ship kernels or maintenance support for that method.

03

### Benchmark on your own workloads [...] TurboQuant.

# TurboQuant vs KIVI

Two methods that solve the same broad problem from different angles. KIVI is a known KV cache quantization baseline. TurboQuant is Google's newer approach extending to vector quantization overhead and vector search.

results.title: TurboQuant: the new(?) and controversial ground breaking compression breakthrough from Google
results.content: The key-value (KV) cache is the memory structure that allows transformer models to “remember” everything they’ve seen in a conversation or document during inference. Without it, the model would have to reprocess the entire context from scratch on every token generation step. The problem is architectural and unforgiving: KV cache memory grows linearly with both sequence length and batch size, which means serving real users at scale pushes it past comfortable limits fast. [...] To make this concrete, consider a 70B parameter model serving 100 concurrent requests at a 32,000-token context window. At standard BF16 precision, the KV cache alone can consume well over 100GB of GPU memory, potentially more than the model weights themselves. That’s not a theoretical edge case; that’s a Tuesday afternoon for anyone running a serious inference cluster. [...] TurboQuant is Google’s proposed approach to one of the most consequential unsolved problems in production large language model efficiency: what do you do when the memory your model needs during inference grows faster than your hardware budget? KV cache compression is where that question gets answered or doesn’t, and TurboQuant claims to have cracked it. Our analysis shows that distinct channels of a key/value activation embedding are highly interdependent, and the joint entropy of multiple channels grows at a slower rate than the sum of their marginal entropy, which implies that per-channel independent quantization is sub-optimal. To mitigate this sub-optimality, we propose Coupled Quantization (CQ), which couples multiple key/value channels together for quantization to exploit [...] Efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) requires batching multiple requests together to improve throughput. As batch size, context length, or model size increases, the size of key and value (KV) cache quickly becomes the main contributor to GPU memory usage and the bottleneck of inference latency and throughput. Quantization has emerged as an effective technique for KV cache compression, but existing methods still fail at very low bit widths. Currently, KV cache quantization is [...] to exploit their interdependence and encode the activations in a more information-efficient manner. Extensive experiments reveal that CQ compares favorably with existing baselines in preserving model quality, and improves inference throughput by 1.4–3.5$\times$ relative to the uncompressed baseline. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CQ can preserve model quality reasonably with KV cache quantized down to 1 bit.
